items.value: Park at Bondi Junction, bus down

blocks.title: Read every sign before you walk off
blocks.text: Inspectors patrol Bondi hard, especially on weekends, and fines add up fast — blocking a driveway is among the priciest mistakes you can make. Time limits, permit-only zones and no-stopping lines change street by street, so read the closest sign before you leave the car.
The free parking that actually exists

Bondi does have genuinely free, unrestricted parking — you just have to walk for it. My go-to is the residential grid north and west of Blair Street, a 6–10 minute stroll from the sand and free around the clock in the unrestricted sections. On weekdays it holds until residents come home in the late afternoon; on sunny weekends it fills from mid-morning, which is exactly why arriving early matters.

One honest caveat: the streets closest to the water slip into resident-permit and timed zones without much warning — Waverley runs Resident Parking Schemes across Bondi, so a free-looking bay can be permit-only. Accept the walk and you'll find far more room.

South Bondi is my secret. Everyone aims for the middle of the beach, so the blocks around Francis Street often have space when the north end is chaos. It's a slightly longer stroll, but I'd rather walk five minutes than do another lap.
Paid parking, closest to furthest
When I don't want the walk — beach gear, kids, a cold day — I pay. Roughly by closeness to the sand:

items: Queen Elizabeth Drive station — Waverley Council's own car park right behind the beach, around 500 bays. The closest and most convenient, and the first to fill on a nice day.
Pacific Bondi car park — opposite the Pavilion, a two-minute walk to the sand. Booking online ahead is usually cheaper than paying the gate rate.
Wilson Parking at The Hub on Hall Street — undercover and often overlooked; handy when the beachfront lots are full, especially for a shorter stay.
On-street meters along Campbell Parade — the most convenient and the priciest per hour, and time-limited, so they suit a quick visit rather than a full beach day.

blocks.title: What will it cost?
blocks.text: Waverley Council sets the meter rates, and they run higher for beach-adjacent bays in summer than for streets further back. The council reviews these fees regularly, so rather than trust a fixed figure — including any you read here — check the current rates on Waverley's parking page and budget for a daily cap.
My busy-day plan, hour by hour

stops.title: Arrive early, park anywhere
stops.detail: Both the free streets and the Queen Elizabeth Drive station still have room. Swim, walk, coffee — you've beaten the crush.

stops.title: The hard window
stops.detail: This is when you'll circle. Arriving now, skip the beachfront and head straight for South Bondi streets, a paid station, or the park-and-ride below.

stops.title: It opens up again
stops.detail: The morning crowd starts leaving and bays free up — perfect for a late swim, sunset and dinner on Hall Street.

blocks.text: If it's a perfect summer Saturday, don't fight it: drive to Bondi Junction, park there, and jump on the 333, 380 or 381 bus down — about a 10–15 minute ride. You'll be on the sand while everyone else is still nosing around the block. Check Transport for NSW for timetables and tap on with an Opal card or contactless.

items.q: Is there free parking at Bondi Beach?
items.a: Yes — the residential streets north and west of Blair Street have free, unrestricted bays about a 6–10 minute walk from the sand. Watch for resident-permit and timed zones nearer the beach, and arrive early on weekends.

items.q: What's the closest car park to Bondi Beach?
items.a: Waverley Council's Queen Elizabeth Drive station, right behind the beach with around 500 bays. It's the first to fill on a sunny day, so arrive early or book a nearby lot online.

items.q: How much does it cost to park at Bondi Beach?
items.a: Waverley Council sets the meter rates — higher for beach-adjacent bays in summer than for streets further back — and the paid stations have daily caps. Rates change, so check the council's parking page before you go.

items.q: When should I arrive to actually find a spot?
items.a: Before 9am or after about 4pm on busy weekends and holidays. The 9am–3pm window is hardest; arriving then, plan on a paid station, South Bondi streets, or the Bondi Junction park-and-ride.

items.q: Is there a park-and-ride option?
items.a: Effectively, yes. Park at or near Bondi Junction and take the 333, 380 or 381 bus down — roughly a 10–15 minute trip, and on a hot weekend genuinely faster than hunting for a beachfront bay.

blocks.text: Parking at Bondi rewards planning more than luck. Come early, know your free streets, keep a paid station and the Bondi Junction bus as backups, and always read the sign. Do that and you'll spend the day in the water, not behind the wheel.

Totti's sits inside The Royal Bondi on Bondi Road, a short stroll up from the sand, and it has become one of those Sydney rooms everyone wants a piece of — sun-warmed, loud in the best way, and built around that famous woodfired bread. No booking? You still have options

blocks.text: Bondi packs one of Sydney's best café scenes into a few walkable streets behind the beach — beachfront brunch rooms, serious coffee windows, and a run of newer openings worth knowing about in 2026. Below is the shortlist I'd hand a visitor: what each place is known for, roughly where it is, and who it suits. I write these as a local curator rather than claiming to have eaten at every one this week, so treat the details as a well-researched starting point and check current hours before a special trip.

blocks.title: A living guide
blocks.text: Bondi's café scene moves fast — hours, menus and even owners change. I last reviewed this in August 2026; confirm anything time-sensitive on the venue's own channels before you go.
Best beachfront cafés for brunch
Speedos Café — North Bondi

Speedos sits up at the quieter North Bondi end (Ramsgate Avenue) with some of the best ocean views of any café on the beach. It's the classic post-swim spot — health-leaning brunch, bowls, pancakes and juices, with window benches looking straight out to the water. Best for: a relaxed, view-first breakfast at the north end.
Chapter One — Campbell Parade

Right on Campbell Parade opposite the sand, Chapter One is a café-meets-wine-bar that's been going since 2012, pouring Allpress coffee alongside an all-day menu. It's an easy, central choice if you want to be directly across from the beach. Best for: an all-rounder in the middle of the action.
bills — Hall Street

The Sydney institution founded by Bill Granger has been on Hall Street (number 79) since 2014, and it's still open and busy. Come for the dishes that made it famous — ricotta hotcakes and sweetcorn fritters — in a light, airy room. Best for: a benchmark Bondi brunch and a bit of Sydney food history.
Best for specialty coffee
Harry's Bondi — Wairoa Avenue

Harry's has been caffeinating Bondi since 1997 and is my pick if coffee is the point. It grew from a hole-in-the-wall into a full café, with batch brew, espresso and cold drip plus a following for its matcha and specialty lattes. Best for: coffee-first locals and a quick, quality cup.
Sonoma — bakery coffee

Sonoma is the well-known Sydney sourdough bakery with a Bondi outpost — a reliable stop for a proper coffee and a pastry or bakery-driven breakfast without the full brunch sit-down. Best for: a quick, high-quality grab-and-go.
Gertrude & Alice — Hall Street

Genuinely one of a kind: a second-hand bookshop and café on Hall Street where you can settle in with Campos coffee, a Middle Eastern-leaning breakfast and a stack of books. It's the antidote to Bondi's see-and-be-seen rooms. Best for: a slow, quiet morning and something different.
Strong all-rounders just back from the sand
Blackwood — Glenayr Avenue

An Eastern Suburbs brunch staple a couple of streets back, Blackwood is known for a seasonal menu that blends Mediterranean and Asian influences — ricotta pancakes, chilli scrambled eggs — with carefully made coffee. Best for: a considered brunch away from the beachfront crush.
Porch and Parlour — North Bondi

A long-running North Bondi favourite (Ramsgate Avenue) built around local produce, with its well-known pea pancakes and a reliably buzzy weekend. It's also one of the better-known dog-friendly spots. Best for: a neighbourhood brunch with the dog in tow.
Newer and more unusual spots
Cafe Bondi — North Bondi (new)

One of the more recent openings, Cafe Bondi is on Campbell Parade at the North Bondi end and opens early for coffee, sunshine and an easy all-day menu. Best for: an early start at the quieter north end. (As a newer venue, double-check its days and hours before you rely on it.)
Up South — Bondi Road

Further up Bondi Road, Up South made its name on playful matcha creations and a rotating treats cabinet — the spot for a strawberry or pistachio matcha and a photo. Best for: matcha fans and a sweet mid-morning stop.
Lox, Stock & Barrel — bagels & deli
A Bondi take on a Jewish deli, known for artisan bagels and generous, deli-influenced brunch plates. Best for: a bagel-led breakfast or an easy weekday lunch.
Makaveli & Pocket — café by day, bar by night

From the same team, Makaveli (Glenayr Avenue) and Pocket (Campbell Parade) both work the café-to-cocktail-bar angle — pastries, loaded sourdough and coffee in the morning, share plates and drinks later. Best for: a laid-back start that can roll into the afternoon.
What's changed recently

Two things worth flagging for 2026. First, there's genuine new blood at the north end — Cafe Bondi being the clearest recent opening. Second, the former Hall Street all-day spot Bondi Hall has closed, so ignore older lists that still feature it. The refurbished Bondi Pavilion has also reopened with food and drink operators on the beachfront; those line-ups have shifted since the works, so check who's trading there now rather than trusting an older guide.
What to know before you go

items: Timing: arrive close to opening or after about 2pm to dodge the worst queues; weekend mornings are the busiest.
Booking: most Bondi cafés are walk-in, though a few take reservations for larger groups — check ahead if there are more than four of you.
Dogs: several are dog-friendly, with Porch and Parlour the best-known; outdoor tables are your friend.
Reusables: bring a keep-cup — some cafés knock a little off for it.
Make a morning of it: pair a café with the Saturday [Bondi Farmers Market](/whats-on/markets), or a swim first — see [where to swim at Bondi](/where-to-swim-at-bondi-beach).

blocks.text: Yes — anyone can swim at the Bondi Icebergs pool. It's a public ocean pool open seven days a week, and you don't need to be a club member to jump in. It's the one you've seen a thousand times on Instagram: two turquoise pools carved into the rocks at the southern end of Bondi, waves crashing straight over the edge. I swim here often, so here are the questions I get asked most, answered honestly — and where a price or time is the sort of thing that changes, I'll point you at the official page rather than risk something stale.
Getting in: hours and fees

The pool opens early — dawn starts most days — and runs into the early evening, seven days a week. It's typically closed on Thursdays for cleaning, though in summer, when the tides cooperate, it often stays open. Opening and closing times shift with the seasons, races and the surf, so rather than quote a clock time that might be stale, I check the official Pool Conditions page at icebergs.com.au the morning I'm heading down.

Entry is casual — no booking, just pay at the kiosk and walk down to the water. There are single passes for adults, children and families, and multi-visit passes that bring the per-swim cost down for regulars. For the current dollar figures, check the Pool Conditions page — prices are exactly the kind of thing I won't quote from memory.

blocks.title: The tide calls the shots
blocks.text: Entry can be affected by tides, swimming races and event days, so the pool occasionally closes to public swimmers at short notice. If you've travelled across town for it, a quick look at the official pool status saves a wasted trip.
What it's actually like to swim here

Two pools sit side by side: a 50-metre lap pool and a smaller, shallower one that's gentler for little kids. The water is ocean-fed and unheated, so the temperature tracks the sea — glorious in late summer, bracing in the best way come winter. On a big swell, waves break clean over the sea wall and wash through the lanes, which is precisely the drama people come for. Lifeguards are on duty during opening hours, but respect the conditions: when it's pumping, the far lanes get lively.

Go early. I love a dawn swim before the crowds — soft light, calm lap lanes, and that postcard shot with the waves over the wall and almost nobody in it. Towel and locker hire are on-site for a small fee, but it's easier to pack your own.
Is there a sauna?

There is, and it's included with your pool admission — a proper reward after a cold-water lap. Sessions are time-capped in the shared space, so don't plan to linger, and you'll want your own towel. It's my favourite winter ritual: freezing dip, warm sauna, repeat.
The club, the restaurant and the history

The pool sits beneath the Bondi Icebergs Club, and the two are separate. Upstairs is the members' club — a relaxed bistro and bar with one of the best views in Sydney, open to visitors as a guest (bring photo ID). Higher still is Icebergs Dining Room and Bar, the fine-dining restaurant that books out well ahead. You can swim without setting foot in either, but that view over a cold drink is hard to beat.

The club dates to 1929, founded by a group of local life savers who wanted to stay fit through winter. Its famous "Rule 15B" required members to swim three Sundays out of four for five years to earn lifetime swimming membership — a wonderfully hard-earned badge of honour. The club bills itself as the only licensed winter swimming club in the world, and the premises you see today reopened after a major redevelopment in the early 2000s.

items.q: Can anyone swim at Bondi Icebergs, or do I need to be a member?
items.a: Anyone can swim. The pool has public entry seven days a week (subject to tides and races) — you just pay at the kiosk. Club membership is a separate thing and isn't needed for a casual swim.

items.q: How much does it cost to swim?
items.a: It's a modest single-visit fee, with cheaper multi-visit passes for regulars. Because prices change, check the official Pool Conditions page at icebergs.com.au for the current figures rather than rely on a number that might be stale.

items.q: Is the pool heated?
items.a: No. Both pools are ocean-fed and unheated, so the water temperature follows the sea — warm in summer, seriously refreshing in winter.

items.q: Why is the pool closed on Thursdays?
items.a: Thursday is the usual cleaning day. In summer, when tides permit, it often stays open on Thursdays too — check the pool status before you go.

items.q: How do I join the Icebergs Winter Swimming Club?
items.a: The winter club is a serious commitment — an induction, a swim time trial and a qualifying season of Sunday swims, not a walk-up membership. If you're keen, contact the club directly through icebergs.com.au for the current process and dates.

blocks.text: That's the honest rundown — whether you're here for one bucket-list dip or a winter regular, the Icebergs lives up to every photo. Pack a towel, check the tide, and I'll see you in the slow lane.

The City2Surf draws tens of thousands of runners every August for its atmosphere, its city-to-sea course, and one very famous hill. Whether it's your first or you're chasing a personal best, a bit of preparation goes a long way. Here are the ten things I'd tell any mate before they line up.
1. Know the course

It's 14 km from the CBD to Bondi. The opening kilometres are fast and net downhill, then around the middle you hit Heartbreak Hill — roughly a 2 km climb from Rose Bay to Vaucluse. Knowing where the hill sits helps you save energy for it instead of blowing up early.
2. Enter early and pick the right wave

Entries open earlier in the year and sell out — the 2026 event sold out well before race day. Register as soon as entries open, and choose a start wave that matches your realistic finish time so you're not weaving through slower runners (or holding up faster ones).
3. Train for the hill

Heartbreak Hill is what people remember. Add hill repeats to your training once a week in the lead-up so both your legs and your head know what a sustained climb feels like. It's the single best thing you can do for your time.
4. Build up gradually

Increase your weekly distance slowly rather than cramming. A mix of one longer run, some faster efforts and easy recovery jogs beats a couple of heroic long runs. Consistency is what gets you to 14 km comfortably.
5. Sort your hydration and fuelling

Hydrate in the days before, not just on the morning. Have a light, familiar breakfast a couple of hours before the start. Whatever gels or drinks you plan to use, practise with them in training first.
6. Gear you've tested — and sunscreen

Wear well-broken-in shoes and light, moisture-wicking clothing. Nothing brand new on race day. And even in August, put on sweat-resistant sunscreen before the start — the sun really shows up by the time you reach Bondi.
7. Plan your transport

Roads close and the nearest stations fill early. Give yourself a solid hour of buffer to get to the start, find the gear check, queue for the loo and warm up. Public transport beats driving every time on race day.
8. Check the weather

Early-August Sydney can swing from cool and grey to surprisingly warm. Check the Bureau of Meteorology forecast and dress accordingly — a cheap layer you can shed at the start line is a good friend on a cold morning.
9. Pace it in thirds

Start conservatively, run the hill on effort rather than staring at your pace, and use the downhills to recover without over-striding. Break the run into thirds and reassess how you feel at each. Negative-splitting the City2Surf feels a lot better than fading.
10. Recover and celebrate

Keep walking for a few minutes after the line rather than stopping dead, grab water and a snack, and agree a meeting spot with your crew in advance — phone signal gets patchy in the crowd. Then reward yourself: brunch, a swim, or a dip at the Icebergs pool. You've earned it.

items.q: How long is the City2Surf and how hilly is it?
items.a: 14 km, and hillier than first-timers expect. The main climb is Heartbreak Hill, about 2 km from Rose Bay to Vaucluse near halfway, with a few more short rises after it.

items.q: Do City2Surf entries sell out?
items.a: Yes — it's very popular and sells out ahead of race day, so enter early through city2surf.com.au and pick a start wave matching your expected finish time.

items.q: What should I not do on race day?
items.a: Don't wear or eat anything you haven't tested in training, don't go out too fast, and don't skip sunscreen — the Sydney sun is strong by the Bondi finish.

blocks.text: Here's my honest answer to the question everyone asks before their first City2Surf: no, you don't need to be a fitness freak to beat Heartbreak Hill — just a handful of weeks of steady, unglamorous practice on gentle hills. It's a long grind rather than a wall, but a little prep turns dread into a shrug.

I've walked, jogged and occasionally staggered up that hill more times than I'd like to admit, and I've watched plenty of first-timers who "hadn't run since school" reach the top grinning. The trick isn't speed — it's showing up a few times a week and letting your legs get used to going uphill.
First, what Heartbreak Hill actually is

Heartbreak Hill is the roughly 2km climb along New South Head Road between Rose Bay and Vaucluse, around the halfway mark of the 14km City2Surf course that runs from the city out to Bondi Beach. It climbs steadily at a gentle-to-moderate average gradient — it earns its name from length, not steepness. The upside for us mortals: once you're over the top, the back half trends downhill toward the coast.

items.label: Character
items.value: Long and steady, not a sprint wall

items.label: You need
items.value: A few weeks of easy hill practice

blocks.text: A relaxed way to prepare (no gym required)

You don't need a rigid program. What works is repetition on small hills, time on your feet, and a couple of simple strength moves — stretch or shorten it to fit your weeks before race day. Step-ups in particular mimic exactly what a climb asks of you.
1. Build the habit

For the first couple of weeks, forget hills and just move four or five days a week. Walk-jog intervals work well: jog 30 seconds, walk 90, repeat for 20–30 minutes. The goal is just to make moving normal again.
2. Add gentle hills

Once that feels easy, find a hill that takes one to two minutes to climb and go up it four to six times, strolling down to recover. Do this once or twice a week — it's the most useful thing you can do, because hills get easier fast when you practise them.
3. Stretch out one longer session

Keep one weekend walk-jog that slowly grows — 4km, then 6km, then 8km — ideally over undulating ground. You're teaching your body to be comfortable on its feet for a couple of hours, which is what a fun run really is.
4. A tiny strength set, twice a week

items: 10 squats
10 lunges per leg
10 step-ups per leg on a park bench or stair
A 20–30 second plank

blocks.text: Train on terrain that isn't boring and you'll actually turn up. The Bondi to Bronte coastal walk has stairs and rises with an ocean view, and Centennial Park's rolling paths suit long walk-jogs. To rehearse the real thing, jog the Rose Bay to Vaucluse climb once before race day.

blocks.title: Check the official details before you commit
blocks.text: Entry dates, prices, start-group waves and the exact course change year to year. Confirm this year's specifics on the official City2Surf website rather than trusting a number you read anywhere, including here.

blocks.title: A quick sensible caveat
blocks.text: This is general encouragement from a local, not medical advice. If you're new to exercise, carrying an injury, or have any heart or health concerns, chat with your GP before you start training.
Race-day tactics for the hill

items: Start slower than feels natural — the hill arrives around the middle of the course, so don't burn your matches early.
Walk it if you want — it's a fun run, and brisk walking uphill is barely slower than a labouring jog.
Shorten your stride, keep your steps quick, and let your arms swing — small steps beat big heavy ones.
Look up the road, not at your feet, and soak up the crowd. The atmosphere genuinely carries you.

blocks.text: You're stronger than you think — the hill is long, but almost nobody around you is really racing it.

items.q: How hard is Heartbreak Hill really?
items.a: More tiring than terrifying. The gradient is gentle-to-moderate; what makes it tough is that it runs around 2km, mid-course, when your legs are already warm. Pace yourself early and plenty of first-timers walk it happily.

items.q: Can I walk City2Surf and still finish?
items.a: Absolutely. Plenty of people walk part or all of it, and the back half trends downhill toward Bondi. Just keep moving.

items.q: How long do I need to train?
items.a: If you can already walk comfortably for an hour, a few weeks of walk-jogs plus a short hill session or two each week makes a real difference. Consistency beats any single long session.

items.q: Where can I practise hills near Bondi?
items.a: The Bondi to Bronte coastal walk has stairs and rises with a view, Centennial Park offers rolling terrain, and the Rose Bay to Vaucluse climb lets you rehearse the real hill.

items.q: Where do I find this year's entry and course details?
items.a: Check the official City2Surf website for the current year's date, entry fees, start groups and course map — those details shift year to year.

blocks.text: So no, you don't have to be a fitness fanatic. Put in a few weeks of easy practice, start race day slower than your ego wants, and let the crowd and the downhill carry you home to Bondi. See you at the finish.

blocks.text: Driving to Tamarama, Coogee or Clovelly on a warm weekend? Here's the short version: on-street parking is free at all three but tightly time-limited, and it fills scandalously early — so arrive before 9am, or don't drive at all. Below, here's where the bays are, how long you can stay, and when to just catch the bus.

items.label: Tamarama
items.value: Waverley Council — very limited on-street bays

items.label: Best free lot

blocks.text: Tamarama: the trickiest of the three

Tamarama is my favourite little cove and the hardest place to park in this whole stretch. It sits in the Waverley Council area, and there simply isn't much room — a handful of bays on the streets around Tamarama Park and Tamarama Marine Drive, and no council beach car park at all. On a sunny Saturday those bays are gone by mid-morning, and circling for one wastes a good beach day.
Most bays in Waverley's beach precincts carry a daytime limit (often signposted 2P), so read the sign before you walk off — limits and hours are actively enforced.

Honestly, I rarely drive to Tamarama. It's about a 10-minute stroll along the coastal walk from Bronte (park up there instead), and the 381 loop from Bondi Junction stops right by the beach — check Transport NSW for times. Either way, you skip the parking lottery entirely.
Coogee: free 4P on-street, plus metered car parks

Coogee and Clovelly both sit in Randwick City Council, which back in January 2021 brought in a 4-hour limit (signed 4P) across its beachside streets. The upshot: on-street parking near Coogee Beach is free, but capped at four hours during enforced hours — fine for a swim and lunch, not a whole lazy day.

items: Free 4P bays run through the streets around the beach — Arden, Beach and Brook Streets and the surrounding grid.
The Coogee Beach and Coogee Oval car parks are metered via the PayStay app — pay only for the time you use and top up from your phone.
Come early. In peak summer the closest bays are taken by 9–10am and you'll be walking in from several blocks back.

blocks.title: Rates change — check before you pay
blocks.text: I won't quote a metered hourly rate, since Randwick reviews them — check the current rate on the meter or PayStay app, and read the sign for enforced hours, as overnight rules differ from daytime.
Clovelly: the easiest place to leave the car

Of the three, Clovelly is where I rate your chances. As well as free 4P on-street bays, there's a free car park on the southern side of the beach, by the grassy park and playground. It still fills on a hot day, but the odds beat Tamarama — and you're steps from that flat-water swimming channel that makes Clovelly so good for kids and nervous swimmers.
If the beachside car park and closest streets are full, drive a few blocks uphill and walk down — the 4P bays extend well back, and a five-minute walk beats a 30-minute crawl.

blocks.title: Good news for 2026
blocks.text: In mid-2026, Randwick councillors voted against introducing visitor pay parking at its beaches (Coogee and Clovelly included), so the free 4P system stays for now. Rules can evolve, so I'll keep this page updated — but for this summer, free-but-timed is the deal.
How I'd actually get there

stops.title: Drive if you must
stops.detail: Aim for the Clovelly beachside car park or an on-street 4P bay while they're still open.

stops.title: Park & walk
stops.detail: Grab any 4P bay a few blocks back and walk in — far less stressful than chasing the front row.

stops.title: Skip the car
stops.detail: Buses run to all three from Bondi Junction; for Tamarama, walk the coastal path from Bronte or Bondi.

items.q: Is parking free at Coogee and Clovelly?
items.a: Yes — on-street parking at both is free, but limited to four hours (signed 4P) during the enforced hours set by Randwick Council. The Coogee Beach and Coogee Oval car parks are metered and paid via the PayStay app. Always read the sign on the pole.

items.q: Where can I park for free at Clovelly Beach?
items.a: There's a free car park on the southern side of Clovelly Beach beside the park, plus free 4P on-street bays through the surrounding streets. Both fill early on hot days, so come before mid-morning.

items.q: Why is Tamarama so hard to park at?
items.a: It's a small cove with only a handful of time-limited on-street bays and no council car park, so on busy days they're taken by mid-morning. I usually walk in along the coastal path from Bronte instead.

items.q: How long can I leave my car?
items.a: Most beachside on-street bays at Coogee and Clovelly are 4-hour (4P) limited during enforced hours; Tamarama's are typically shorter (often 2P). Check the exact limit on the signpost, as they're actively enforced.

items.q: Is it worth driving, or should I catch public transport?
items.a: On summer weekends I'd catch the bus — all three are served from Bondi Junction, and for Tamarama the coastal walk from Bronte beats hunting for a bay. Driving only pays off before 9am.

blocks.text: So there it is — free but timed at all three, easiest at Clovelly, near-impossible at Tamarama on a hot day. Get in early, read the sign, or let the bus do the work.

blocks.text: If you want a scroll from Sundays Bondi without wasting your whole morning in a line, the short answer is this: go early, go on a day they've actually announced they're open, and know exactly what you're ordering before you reach the window. Sundays is the tiny micro-bakery at 211 Bondi Road that founder Laetitia Loefti turned into a genuine phenomenon, and on a good day it can sell out within about an hour of opening. Here's how I'd play it.
First, the thing nobody tells you: check the hours before you leave

This is the single most important tip. Sundays opens a limited number of days a week — usually weekend mornings from 9am until 2pm or until they sell out — but the exact days have shifted since they opened, and I've seen listings disagree on which days they trade. So don't take my word for it or an old blog post's: open their Instagram (@sundaysbondi) the night before and confirm they're baking. It's a two-minute check that saves a wasted trip across town.

blocks.title: They genuinely do sell out
blocks.text: On busy days Sundays has cleared out well before the 2pm close — reports from opening weekend had them gone within the first hour. If you turn up at lunchtime expecting a leisurely scroll, there's a real chance the case is empty. Treat the posted closing time as a maximum, not a guarantee.
What to order

The scrolls here aren't your dense, heavy bakery version — they're light and airy, almost pancake-like, because the dough is cold-fermented overnight and given extra time to rise before baking. That texture is the whole point, so order at least one classic to understand what the fuss is about.

items: Classic cinnamon with cream cheese — the signature and the one I'd never skip. Order it first; it goes first.
Biscoff — one of the core flavours, rich and caramelised if you like things sweeter.
Kinder chocolate — the other regular in the rotation, and a hit with kids (and, honestly, most adults).
Rotating specials like pistachio — these are the ones that vanish fastest, so grab one if it's on the day you visit.
Matcha — Sundays leans hard into matcha, so a matcha scroll or matcha drink alongside your cinnamon is the classic Bondi order.

blocks.text: Prices sit at the premium end for a scroll, which is what you'd expect from small-batch baking with good ingredients. Rather than quote a number that may have moved, I'd just check the board on the day — but go in expecting boutique-bakery pricing, not servo-pastry pricing.

Seating is tiny to non-existent, so I always get mine takeaway and walk the five-ish minutes down Bondi Road to the promenade. A warm cinnamon scroll eaten on the grass above the sand, coffee in hand, is one of my favourite cheap-thrill Bondi mornings.
How I'd time a queue-free-ish visit

stops.title: Check Instagram
stops.detail: Confirm @sundaysbondi is open the next day and note the flavours they're teasing.

stops.title: Arrive before opening
stops.detail: The line starts before the doors do. Being there before 9am is the difference between first batch and no batch.

stops.title: Order everything you want in one go
stops.detail: Know your order before you reach the window — it keeps the line moving and means you won't miss out on a special.

stops.title: Walk it to the beach
stops.detail: Takeaway down Bondi Road to the promenade and eat with a view instead of squeezing inside.

blocks.text: Getting there

Sundays sits at 211 Bondi Road, roughly halfway between Bondi Junction and the beach. Buses run frequently along Bondi Road from Bondi Junction interchange (which connects to the train line), and it's an easy walk up from the sand. Parking is metered and competitive on weekends, so if you can avoid driving, do — plug '211 Bondi Road' into the Transport for NSW trip planner for live bus times.

items.q: What days is Sundays Bondi open?
items.a: It's a limited-days micro-bakery — generally weekend mornings from 9am to 2pm or until sold out — but the days have changed since opening and different listings disagree. Always confirm on their Instagram (@sundaysbondi) before you make the trip.

items.q: What time should I arrive to beat the queue?
items.a: Before 9am. On busy days the first batch can be gone quickly and they've sold out within about an hour, so arriving right at (or just before) opening gives you the best shot at the full range of flavours.

items.q: What should I order at Sundays Bondi?
items.a: Start with the classic cinnamon scroll with cream cheese — it's the signature. The core line-up also includes Biscoff and Kinder chocolate, plus rotating specials like pistachio, and matcha in both scroll and drink form.

items.q: Do they sell out?
items.a: Yes, regularly, often well before the posted 2pm close. Treat closing time as a maximum and go early rather than turning up at lunch and hoping.

items.q: Where exactly is Sundays Bondi?
items.a: 211 Bondi Road, Bondi — about halfway between Bondi Junction and Bondi Beach, walkable from the promenade and served by buses running along Bondi Road.

blocks.text: That's the whole game with Sundays: it's small, it's genuinely good, and it rewards a bit of planning. Check they're open, show up early, know your order, and take it down to the beach. Do that and you'll skip the disappointment I see on faces at 1pm — and you'll understand why the line forms in the first place.

blocks.text: The lifeguards you know from Bondi Rescue are real professional lifeguards employed by Waverley Council, not actors — the same crew in blue and yellow who patrol Bondi Beach every day of the year. The TV show made them household names, but their day job is keeping one of the world's busiest beaches safe. Here's who the best-known lifeguards are, some facts about the show, and how to see the team in action. The roster changes over the seasons, so I keep this updated as things shift.

blocks.title: A note I keep current
blocks.text: Lifeguard line-ups rotate and some faces move on, so treat the bios below as the well-known regulars rather than a live roster. I last reviewed this in August 2026.
What is Bondi Rescue?

Bondi Rescue is the documentary series that follows the Waverley Council lifeguards through the Australian summer. It first aired in 2006 on Network 10, is made by production company CJZ, and has run for around 18 seasons — one of Australia's longest-running and most-exported factual shows, screening in dozens of countries. It was rested in 2025 (no new season that year) and, according to its producers, is expected to return, with filming subject to arrangements with Waverley Council. Either way, the lifeguards themselves keep patrolling Bondi.
The Bondi lifeguards you'll recognise
Bruce ‘Hoppo’ Hopkins — head lifeguard

Hoppo is the head lifeguard and the show's steady centre of gravity. He's been part of the Bondi lifeguard service since the early 1990s, and on screen he's the calm, experienced voice coordinating the team through busy days and serious rescues. If there's one name people associate with Bondi Rescue, it's his.
Anthony ‘Harries’ Carroll

Harries is one of the show's most recognisable and charismatic lifeguards — high-energy, endlessly committed on a rescue, and known for his fundraising and community antics off the sand. He's one of the longest-serving faces of the team.
Andrew ‘Reidy’ Reid
Reidy is a seasoned member of the crew, known on the show for his humour and his fitness, with a strong social-media following. He's one of the regulars viewers have followed across many seasons.
Trent ‘Maxi’ Maxwell

Maxi came through as one of the younger lifeguards and became a fan favourite. He's also widely known for working as a firefighter — splitting his time between saving lives on the beach and in the city.
Dean ‘Deano’ Gladstone
Deano is another long-serving member of the team who's featured across many seasons of the show.

Plenty of other lifeguards have featured over the years — you'll hear nicknames like Jesse, Chappo, Whippet, Yatesy, Mouse and Kobi among them. Because the team rotates season to season, I focus above on the best-known regulars rather than trying to list everyone currently rostered.
Interesting facts about Bondi Rescue

items: The lifeguards are real Waverley Council employees — professional, paid lifeguards, not actors and not the same thing as the volunteer surf lifesavers in the red-and-yellow caps.
Bondi is one of the most rescue-heavy beaches in Australia, largely thanks to a notorious rip at the south end nicknamed the ‘Backpackers' Express’.
The show is filmed across the Australian summer, when Bondi's crowds — and the number of rescues — peak.
Bondi Rescue has been sold to dozens of countries, making Bondi's lifeguards internationally famous.

For the full run-down, see our companion pieces on [20 obscure facts about Bondi Rescue](/bondi-blog/2023/9/5/20-obscure-facts-about-bondi-rescue) and [the most dramatic moments on the show](/bondi-blog/2025/1/12/the-20-most-dramatic-moments-on-bondi-rescue).

blocks.text: Key moments from the show

Across its seasons Bondi Rescue has captured everything from huge multi-swimmer rescues on wild-surf days to tense resuscitations, shark alarms clearing the water, and the occasional celebrity spotting on the sand. Rather than rank them here, I've pulled the standouts together in a dedicated guide — see [the 20 most dramatic moments on Bondi Rescue](/bondi-blog/2025/1/12/the-20-most-dramatic-moments-on-bondi-rescue).
Can you meet the Bondi lifeguards?

Yes — the lifeguards are on Bondi Beach every day, based around the lifeguard tower towards the south end near the flags. You'll often see the Bondi Rescue crew there in season. A few things I'd keep in mind: they're working, and their first job is watching the water, so give them space during busy periods and never interrupt a rescue for a photo. Swim between the red-and-yellow flags and you're in the patch they're actively watching. The team also has official merchandise and an active social presence if you want to follow along.

blocks.title: Swim between the flags
blocks.text: The best way to respect the lifeguards' work is simple: always swim between the red-and-yellow flags, where they've judged it safest and are watching. See our guide to [where to swim at Bondi](/where-to-swim-at-bondi-beach) for the safest spots.

items.q: Are the Bondi Rescue lifeguards real?
items.a: Yes. They're real professional lifeguards employed by Waverley Council who patrol Bondi Beach year-round. The show is a documentary series, not scripted drama, and the rescues are real.

items.q: Who is the head lifeguard at Bondi?
items.a: Bruce ‘Hoppo’ Hopkins is the long-serving head lifeguard and the most recognisable figure from the show, part of the Bondi service since the early 1990s.

items.q: Is Bondi Rescue still on?
items.a: The show was rested in 2025 with no new season that year, but its producers have said it's expected to return, subject to arrangements with Waverley Council. The lifeguards continue to patrol Bondi regardless.

items.q: Are Bondi lifeguards the same as surf lifesavers?
items.a: No. The Bondi Rescue lifeguards are paid, professional council lifeguards. Volunteer surf lifesavers (in the red-and-yellow caps) are a separate service that also patrols, typically on weekends and public holidays.

items.q: Can I meet the Bondi Rescue lifeguards?
items.a: You can usually see the team around the lifeguard tower on Bondi Beach in season. Be respectful — they're working and watching the water — and never interrupt a rescue.

blocks.text: However you know them — from the tower or the TV — Bondi's lifeguards are a huge part of what makes the beach what it is. For more, see the [Bondi Rescue hub](/bondi-rescue), our guide to [where to swim safely at Bondi](/where-to-swim-at-bondi-beach), and the rest of [things to do in Bondi](/things-to-do-in-bondi).

blocks.text: Yes — anyone can swim at the Bondi Icebergs pool. It's the question I get asked most, usually by someone squinting up at that famous ocean pool and assuming it must be a members-only club. It isn't. The Icebergs Club upstairs has members, but the pool below is open to the public seven days a week — you pay at the door and walk down to the water. Here's what I'd want a friend to know before their first swim.

items.label: Where
items.value: 1 Notts Ave, southern end of Bondi Beach

items.label: Pools
items.value: 50m saltwater lap pool + shallow kids' pool

items.label: Lifeguards
items.value: On patrol during opening hours, year-round

blocks.text: So who can actually swim here?

Everyone. Kids, grandparents, first-timers, serious squad swimmers doing their pre-dawn laps — I've shared the water with all of them. You don't need to be a member of the Icebergs Club and you don't need to book. You simply turn up, pay the entry fee at the kiosk, and head down to the pool deck. There's a 50-metre saltwater lap pool for proper swimming and a smaller, shallower pool that's perfect for little ones and anyone who just wants a gentle dip.

The one thing worth knowing: this is an ocean pool, not a heated indoor lane pool. On a calm day it's glassy and gorgeous. When there's a big swell running, waves break clean over the eastern wall and the water gets lively — bracing, salty and genuinely wonderful, but something to respect if you're not a confident swimmer. Qualified lifeguards patrol during opening hours all year round, so you're in good hands, but always swim within your ability.
Hours, fees and the famous Thursday closure

The pool opens early — from 6am on weekdays and 6.30am on weekends — and runs through to early evening. The catch every visitor needs to hear: Icebergs closes on Thursdays for its weekly clean, when the pool is drained, scrubbed and refilled with fresh seawater. In summer it can reopen once the tide cooperates, but I'd never bank on it. If your only free day is a Thursday, check the official site first.

blocks.title: Don't get caught out on a Thursday
blocks.text: The regular Thursday cleaning closure is the number-one reason visitors turn up to a closed pool. Hours, tide-related closures and swim-race days can all change, so check the current status on the Bondi Icebergs pool-conditions page before you go.

There is a modest entry fee that goes towards maintaining the pool, with separate adult, child and family rates, plus discounted multi-visit passes if you're staying a while. Prices do get reviewed from time to time, so rather than quote a number that might be stale by the time you read this, I'd point you straight to the Icebergs pool-conditions page for the current rates. Towel and locker hire is available on the day if you've travelled light.

Come mid-morning on a clear day and swim east-to-west so you're looking back at the beach and the Icebergs building on your return lap — it's the best free view in Bondi. And go early if you want the deck quiet; by late morning in summer it fills up fast.
What else is down there

Your entry gets you the pools, changing rooms, showers and the sauna (bring a towel; there's a time limit) — a proper treat after a cold-season swim. On the deck overlooking the water is The Crabbe Hole, a tiny café that does excellent coffee and a good post-swim snack. The upstairs Icebergs Dining Room and bar are a separate operation with their own hours if you fancy a longer sit-down with the view.

items: Bring swimmers, a towel, and cash or card for entry
Goggles are worth it — it's saltwater, and the sun sits low over the water morning and evening

items.q: Do you have to be a member to swim at Bondi Icebergs?
items.a: No. The pool is open to the public seven days a week — you just pay the entry fee at the kiosk. Membership relates to the Icebergs Club upstairs, not to using the pool.

items.q: Is Bondi Icebergs pool open every day?
items.a: It's open daily except Thursdays, when it closes for its weekly clean and refill. In summer it sometimes reopens on Thursday afternoon if the tide allows, but that's never guaranteed — check the official pool-conditions page.

items.q: How much does it cost to swim at Bondi Icebergs?
items.a: There's a small entry fee with separate adult, child and family rates and cheaper multi-visit passes. Because prices are reviewed periodically, check the current rates on the Icebergs pool-conditions page rather than relying on an old figure.

items.q: Is the Icebergs pool safe for kids and beginners?
items.a: There's a shallow children's pool alongside the 50m lap pool, and lifeguards patrol during opening hours. It is an ocean pool, though, so on big-swell days waves wash over the wall — keep a close eye on little ones and swim within your limits.

items.q: Is Bondi Icebergs pool heated?
items.a: No — it's an unheated saltwater ocean pool filled from the sea, so it's refreshingly cool. The on-site sauna, included with entry, is the classic way to warm up before or after your swim.

blocks.text: So next time you're on the promenade wondering whether that iconic pool is off-limits — it isn't. Grab your swimmers, check it's not a Thursday, and go have one of the best swims of your life.

Looking for City2Surf results from a particular year between 2000 and 2024? The quickest way to find your own finish time or bib number is the official City2Surf results portal at city2surf.com.au, which lets you search past events by name — and for the deep historical picture, the Ausrunning archive tracks placings and times back to the very first run. Below are the landmarks that actually matter, and where to dig for the year you want.
Where to find your result, year by year

I get asked this a lot, usually by someone who ran once years ago and wants to prove to their kids they did it. The good news: the results don't disappear. Rather than re-type tens of thousands of times and inevitably get one wrong, here's where the accurate records live:

items: Official results search — city2surf.com.au keeps a searchable database of past events. Search by first and last name, or by bib number if you still have it.
Ausrunning's archive — a runner-maintained record of placings and elite times back to 1971, handy for comparing winners and fields across the decades.
Your confirmation email or charity page — if you fundraised through the official platform, your entry and result are usually linked to that account.

blocks.text: Names get entered exactly as you registered them, so if a search comes up empty, try a nickname, a maiden name, or your surname alone. Misspelled and hyphenated names are the top reason people think their result 'vanished'.
The records that have stood the whole time

Here's what surprises people scrolling through 2000 to 2024: the outright course records were both set outside that window and never beaten since. So across every year in this archive, runners were chasing times already on the books.

Susie Power's 45:08 in 2001 sits at the start of this archive's range and remains the women's benchmark. Steve Moneghetti's 40:02 from 1991 — set by one of the race's most dominant men's champions — is the one the elite men still measure themselves against. If you ever want to feel humble about your own time, remember they ran that including Heartbreak Hill.
How the field changed from 2000 to 2024

The bigger story of these years isn't the pointy end — it's the sheer scale. Through the 2000s the event ballooned into the largest timed fun run of its kind in the world, cresting around 80,000 entrants for its 40th anniversary in 2010. Colour-coded start waves, seeded by expected finish time, became the norm because that many people can't all leave the line at once. For most of us the result that matters isn't a podium place — it's beating last year, or finally running the whole hill.

blocks.title: A note on exact yearly times
blocks.text: I haven't reproduced full winner lists or splits for every year here — those numbers shift with re-timings and corrections, and I won't publish a figure I can't stand behind. For the definitive time in any given year, use the official results search or the Ausrunning archive in my sources.
Reading your result like a local

When you pull up an old result, look past the gun time. Your net (chip) time — from when you actually crossed the start mat — is the fairer number if you started in a back wave. Your category placing shows how you fared against your own age group, not the elites. And if you ran more than one year, line the net times up side by side: that's the real story of your City2Surf.

items.q: Where can I find City2Surf results for a specific year like 2019 or 2024?
items.a: Use the official results search at city2surf.com.au and enter your name or bib number, choosing the event year you want. For historical placings and elite times going back decades, the Ausrunning City to Surf archive is the most complete public record.

items.q: What is the City2Surf course record?
items.a: The men's record is 40:02, set by Steve Moneghetti in 1991; the women's is 45:08, set by Susie Power in 2001. Both were set at or before the start of this 2000–2024 archive and still stand.

items.q: Why can't I find my result in the search?
items.a: Almost always it's a name mismatch. Try your surname alone, any nickname or maiden name you may have registered under, and double-check the year. If you have your old bib number, searching by that is the most reliable method.

items.q: How long is the City2Surf and where does it finish?
items.a: It's about 14 km (officially 13.907 km), running from Sydney's CBD out to the finish at Bondi Beach, with the famous Heartbreak Hill climb near the halfway point.

items.q: How many people run the City2Surf?
items.a: It's grown into the largest fun run of its kind in the world, reaching around 80,000 entrants by its 40th anniversary in 2010, which is why runners set off in staggered, colour-coded start waves.

blocks.text: So whether you're reliving a glory day from 2004 or checking your split from 2023, the records are there and searchable. Find your time, be proud of it, and if it's been a while — maybe this August is the year to add a fresh line to your own archive.

blocks.text: The quickest way from Sydney Airport to Bondi Beach is a taxi or rideshare, which takes roughly 30 to 50 minutes depending on traffic; the cheapest is the train to Bondi Junction followed by a short bus, which usually runs around 60 to 90 minutes door to door. I've done this run more times than I can count picking up friends and family, so here's exactly how I'd get you from the terminal to the sand.

items.label: You'll need
items.value: An Opal card or a contactless card/phone

blocks.text: Train to Bondi Junction, then a bus (my pick for value)

Bondi Beach doesn't have its own train station — the closest is Bondi Junction, about 3 km up the hill. From either the Domestic (T2/T3) or International (T1) terminal, follow the signs to the station right under the terminal and catch the T8 Airport & South Line towards the city. At Central, change to the T4 Eastern Suburbs & Illawarra Line and ride it to Bondi Junction. The T8 runs frequently every day from roughly 5am to midnight, so you rarely wait long.

At Bondi Junction, walk up to the bus interchange above the station and jump on the 333, 380 or 381 — all three run down to Bondi Beach in about 10 to 15 minutes. Tap the same Opal card or contactless card/phone on and off and you're done.

blocks.title: Watch the airport Station Access Fee
blocks.text: Both airport stations charge a Station Access Fee on top of your normal fare — it's a significant extra per adult trip and it sits OUTSIDE the daily and weekly Opal travel caps. It also isn't covered by the 60-minute transfer discount. Check the current amount on the Opal website before you budget, as it changes each year.

If you're travelling light and want to dodge the airport rail fee, locals sometimes walk a few minutes to the public bus stops outside the terminal and take a bus to nearby Mascot station, then ride the T8 from there — the ordinary train fare, no access fee. Use the Transport NSW Trip Planner on the day to check the current stop and route.
Taxi or rideshare (fastest, door to door)

If you've got luggage, kids, or you land late, I'd just take a taxi or an Uber/rideshare. It's the only truly door-to-door option and drops you right at your accommodation. Taxis queue at the rank outside each terminal; rideshare has its own signed pickup zones — follow the app. Expect somewhere in the 30 to 50 minute range depending on traffic and time of day.

blocks.title: On price
blocks.text: Taxis run on a metered fare, and rideshare quotes you before you confirm. I won't put a fixed dollar figure here because both move with traffic, time of day and demand surges. A metered taxi and an off-peak rideshare are usually in a similar ballpark; rideshare can spike at busy times, so check the in-app quote first.
Other options: shuttle, private transfer and car hire

items: Door-to-door shuttles and pre-booked private transfers exist and can be handy for groups or early flights — book ahead and confirm the price when you reserve.
Hiring a car makes sense only if you're touring beyond Sydney. Around Bondi, parking is tight and metered, so a car you're not using is more hassle than help.
Route 350 bus links the Domestic terminal directly to Bondi Junction if you'd rather skip the train — then it's the 333/380/381 down to the beach.

stops.detail: Head up to the bus interchange above the station.

items.q: Is there a train station at Bondi Beach?
items.a: No. The nearest station is Bondi Junction, around 3 km from the sand. From there it's a 10 to 15 minute bus (333, 380 or 381) or a short taxi ride down to the beach.

items.q: What's the cheapest way from the airport to Bondi?
items.a: Public transport: the T8 train to Central, change to the T4 to Bondi Junction, then a bus to the beach. Just note the airport Station Access Fee adds a fixed charge on top of the fare — check the current amount on the Opal website.

items.q: How long does it take?
items.a: Roughly 30 to 50 minutes by taxi or rideshare, and about 60 to 90 minutes by train and bus once you factor in connections and waiting time.

items.q: Do I need an Opal card?
items.a: You don't need a physical Opal card — you can tap on and off with a contactless credit/debit card or a phone/watch. Adult fares are the same either way.

items.q: Can I get a direct bus from the airport?
items.a: There's no single bus straight to Bondi Beach, but Route 350 connects the Domestic terminal to Bondi Junction, where you swap to the 333, 380 or 381 for the beach. Use the Transport NSW Trip Planner for live times.

blocks.text: However you come in, the moment you crest the hill and Campbell Parade opens onto that big blue arc of beach, you'll know the journey was worth it. See you down there.

blocks.text: The simplest way to get to Bondi Beach without a car is to catch a train to Bondi Junction and hop on a bus down the hill — the 333, 380 or 381 will drop you right on Campbell Parade. It's one of my favourite things about living here: for a beach this famous, Bondi is genuinely easy to reach from almost anywhere in Sydney, and you don't need to hire a car to do it.

There's no train station at the beach itself (a common surprise for first-timers), so nearly every public-transport route funnels through Bondi Junction first. Here's exactly how I'd do it, whether you're coming from the CBD, the airport, or driving in for the day.
By public transport (my usual pick)

From the city, take a T4 Eastern Suburbs line train to Bondi Junction — the end of the line and a big interchange. Follow the signs down to the bus stands, where the 333, 380 and 381 all run to Bondi Beach and back. The 333 is the frequent, limited-stops service and the one I aim for; the 380 and 381 stop more often. All three end up at the same place: Campbell Parade, right across from the sand.

The 333 and 380 also run all the way from the CBD (Circular Quay through to Bondi Beach), so if you'd rather stay on one bus the whole way you can skip the train entirely. It's slower than train-then-bus, but you get the harbour-to-ocean view for the trouble.

On a hot summer weekend, the bus down from Bondi Junction can crawl and fill up fast. If it's a gorgeous day and you're able, the walk from Bondi Junction to the beach is roughly 25–30 minutes downhill — sometimes genuinely quicker than waiting for a packed bus, and a nice way to arrive.
Paying your fare

You don't need a paper ticket, and drivers don't sell them. Just tap on with an Opal card or any contactless card or phone (Apple Pay, Google Pay and the like) as you board. On buses you tap on only. Opal cards are sold at convenience stores, supermarkets and stations if you'd prefer one, but for most visitors the card already in your pocket is the easiest option. Fares are distance-based and there are daily and weekly caps — check Transport for NSW for the current amounts before you travel.

blocks.title: Coming from Sydney Airport?
blocks.text: Take the train from the airport to Central, then change to a T4 train to Bondi Junction, and finish on a 333/380/381 bus. Note the airport stations charge an extra station-access fee on top of the normal fare — that's an airport thing, not a Bondi thing.
By car (and the parking reality)

Driving is easy enough — Bondi sits only a handful of kilometres east of the CBD — but I'll be honest about parking, because it's the catch. There's metered street parking around Campbell Parade and the surrounding streets plus a car park behind the beach, but on any warm weekend it fills early and you'll be circling. Most of the metered spots are paid and time-limited, so read the signs carefully and check current rates and time limits with Waverley Council.

If you're set on driving in summer, arrive before about 9am or you'll spend your morning hunting for a space. Better yet, park at Bondi Junction and bus or walk down — it saves the beachfront scramble entirely.
By rideshare or taxi

Uber, taxis and other rideshare services all serve Bondi and will take you door to sand. It's the most convenient option if you're carrying gear or travelling as a group, though fares climb with demand — expect to pay noticeably more on hot afternoons and event weekends when everyone's heading the same way.

items.q: Is there a train station at Bondi Beach?
items.a: No. The closest station is Bondi Junction on the T4 line, about 3km uphill from the sand. From there you take a 333, 380 or 381 bus, or walk down in roughly 25–30 minutes.

items.q: Which bus goes to Bondi Beach?
items.a: The 333, 380 and 381 all run to Bondi Beach. From Bondi Junction any of them work; the 333 is the fastest as it makes fewer stops. The 333 and 380 also run all the way from the CBD.

items.q: Do I need an Opal card, or can I tap my phone?
items.a: Either works. You can tap on with a physical Opal card or with a contactless bank card or phone wallet — same fares and the same daily caps. On buses you only tap on.

items.q: How long does it take to get to Bondi from the city?
items.a: Allow roughly 40–50 minutes by train-then-bus from the CBD, longer on busy summer weekends when traffic and crowds slow the buses down. Check Transport for NSW's trip planner for live times.

items.q: Is it worth driving to Bondi Beach?
items.a: Only if you arrive early. Parking is metered, time-limited and fills fast on warm days. Public transport is usually the less stressful choice — or park at Bondi Junction and finish the trip by bus.

blocks.text: However you come, my advice is the same: travel light, go early on a summer weekend, and let the bus or train do the work so you can save your energy for the water. Bondi's genuinely one of the easiest world-famous beaches to reach — the hardest part is leaving.

blocks.text: I hear it mangled at least once a day down at the beach, usually from a visitor asking directions. So let me settle it for you: Bondi is said "BON-dye" — the last bit rhymes with "eye", not "ee".

For Australians who grew up with Bondi, there's no question about it — but the spelling trips up overseas visitors, who very reasonably read the "i" on the end as "ee". It isn't. Think "bond" (like a secret agent) followed by "eye", with the emphasis on that first syllable: BON-dye.
What "Bondi" actually means

The name is Aboriginal. Waverley Council, which looks after the beach, records that Bondi comes from a local Aboriginal word meaning "the sound of the waves breaking on the beach" (you'll also see it given as "water breaking over rocks"). Once you know that, the name makes perfect sense — stand on the promenade for a minute and the meaning is all around you.
Easy way to lock it in: it rhymes with "Aussie hi" — Bon-dye, not Bon-dee. Get the ending right and you'll sound like you've been coming here for years.

items.q: How do you pronounce Bondi?
items.a: "BON-dye" — "bond" followed by "eye", with the stress on the first syllable. The "i" at the end sounds like "eye", not "ee".

items.q: Is it BON-dee or BON-dye?
items.a: BON-dye. "BON-dee" is the most common mispronunciation among overseas visitors, but locals say BON-dye.

items.q: What does Bondi mean?
items.a: It's from a local Aboriginal word. Waverley Council records the meaning as "the sound of the waves breaking on the beach" (also commonly translated as "water breaking over rocks").

blocks.text: Hope that helps — now say it with confidence and enjoy the beach.

Let me save you the goosebumps: no, the Bondi Icebergs pool is not heated. It's an ocean pool, filled straight from the Tasman Sea, so whatever the water is doing out the front of Bondi that day is pretty much what you'll be diving into. On a still February morning that's glorious. In the depths of a Sydney winter, it's the sort of cold that makes you gasp, laugh, and feel very alive — which, honestly, is the whole point of the place.

items.label: Water
items.value: Natural saltwater, fed by the sea

blocks.text: So how cold does it actually get?

Because the pool takes its water from the ocean, its temperature tracks the sea temperature off Bondi. Broadly, the water is warmest in late summer (roughly December to March) and coldest in winter (around June to August). On a warm, sunny day the shallow ends can take the edge off as the sun works on them, but don't expect a spa — the sea sets the tone here, not a boiler.

blocks.title: Want the real number before you go?
blocks.text: Sea temperature swings from day to day with tides, swell and wind. Rather than trust a figure that's weeks out of date, check the Bureau of Meteorology's Sydney sea-temperature reading, or the club's own Pool Conditions page, on the morning of your swim.

Every so often a big swell washes right over the edge and floods the pool with fresh, cold ocean water — part of what keeps it so clean, and part of why the temperature can shift between visits. It's a living pool, not a climate-controlled one.
Why isn't it heated — and why locals love that

Icebergs earned its name honestly. The winter swimming club that gives the place its identity has been meeting here since 1929, and the tradition is built on cold water: members famously swim right through winter, and the folklore is that they'd drop actual blocks of ice into the pool to keep the season honest. Heating it would rather miss the point. For a lot of us, that bracing hit of cold saltwater — with waves crashing over the sea wall beside you and the whole sweep of Bondi in front — is exactly what makes a lap here feel different from any indoor pool.

If you feel the cold, go for a mid-to-late morning swim on a sunny day, when the sun has been on the water for a few hours and the wind is usually lightest. Bring a towel you can wrap up in fast, and a coffee from the promenade afterwards is non-negotiable.
Warming up: is there anything heated here?

The swimming is cold, but the building above it is not. The Icebergs complex houses a sauna and hot showers, plus the club and the well-known dining room upstairs, so you can thaw out and look back down over the pool you just braved. If a heated indoor swim is what you're truly after, Bondi's ocean pools aren't it — you'd want a standard indoor aquatic centre elsewhere. Icebergs is about the ocean, cold and honest.

items.q: Is the Bondi Icebergs pool heated?
items.a: No. It's an unheated ocean pool filled with natural saltwater straight from the sea, so its temperature follows the ocean — warmest in summer, genuinely cold in winter.

items.q: How cold is Icebergs in winter?
items.a: Cold enough to take your breath away — it mirrors the winter sea temperature off Bondi. For the actual reading on any given day, check the Bureau of Meteorology's Sydney sea temperature or the club's Pool Conditions page before you go.

items.q: Is the water salt or chlorine?
items.a: Saltwater. The pool is fed directly by the ocean rather than treated with chlorine like a suburban pool, which is a big part of its character.

items.q: Is there anywhere warm to recover after a swim?
items.a: Yes — the Icebergs complex has a sauna and hot showers, and the club and dining room upstairs are a lovely spot to warm up with a view over the pool.

items.q: Can I still swim there in winter?
items.a: Absolutely — winter swimming is the whole tradition at Icebergs. The pool is open to the public year-round; just check current hours and any cleaning-day closures on the official Icebergs website first.

blocks.text: My honest advice? Don't let "unheated" put you off. Pick a bright morning, walk down the steps, and take the plunge — cold water and all. It's one of those Bondi experiences that's far better felt than described, and you'll be talking about it long after you've warmed up.

blocks.text: If you only have time for one, come at sunrise. Bondi faces almost due east onto the Pacific, so the sun climbs straight out of the ocean here — the best light show the beach gives you all day. Sunset is a quieter, sneakier pleasure: the sun drops behind the suburbs at your back, but the sky and the sandstone cliffs catch a soft pink glow I love just as much. Here are my favourite spots for both, and how to time them.

items.label: Sunrise
items.value: Over the ocean — the main event

items.label: Sunset
items.value: Behind you; watch the afterglow on the cliffs

blocks.text: Where I go for sunrise
The whole eastern edge of Bondi is a front-row seat, but a few spots lift it from lovely to unforgettable.
Mackenzies Point (the south headland)

This is my desert-island pick. From the clifftop lookout at the southern end of the beach — the first headland on the Bondi to Bronte walk — you look back across the whole arc of sand with the sun coming up over the water beyond Ben Buckler. The sandstone catches the first light beautifully, and roughly between May and November you've a genuine chance of spotting migrating whales offshore while you wait.
Bondi Icebergs and the south corner

You don't need to be swimming to get the shot every visitor wants: the ocean pool in the foreground, waves washing over its edge, sky on fire behind. Stand on the promenade above the pool at the south end of the beach. If you want to swim laps at first light, check the Icebergs website for current pool session times first — they change seasonally and the pool shuts for cleaning.
North Bondi and Ben Buckler

The northern end is calmer and less photographed. The rocks below the North Bondi headland and around Ben Buckler give you crashing surf in the foreground and an open eastern horizon — a peaceful alternative when the south corner is busy.

Check the exact sunrise time the night before (Geoscience Australia's sun times tool is spot-on for Sydney) and arrive 30–40 minutes early. The richest colour — the 'blue hour' and first pink — comes well before the sun clears the horizon, and the best clifftop parking fills fast on clear mornings.
Sunset at an east-facing beach

Here's what nobody tells you: you won't see the sun sink into the sea at Bondi, because it sets behind the land to the west. So chase the afterglow instead. As the sun drops at your back, the eastern sky over the ocean turns soft lilac and rose, and the cliffs and the pale Icebergs building light up gold. Marks Park, on the grassy clifftop just past Mackenzies Point, is my go-to — spread a picnic, face the sea, and watch the colour deepen.

blocks.title: For actual sunset-over-water
blocks.text: If watching the sun drop into the horizon is the whole point for you, Sydney's west-facing harbour spots do it far better than any east-coast beach. At Bondi, come for the sunrise and stay for the afterglow — that's what this coastline does best.
A simple golden-hour plan

blocks.title: Mind the edge
blocks.text: The clifftop lookouts are unfenced in places and the rock platforms below can be hit by sudden waves. Stay back from wet rock and the edge in low light, and never turn your back on the surf for a photo.

items.q: Can you watch the sun set over the ocean at Bondi Beach?
items.a: No — Bondi faces east, so the sun rises over the water and sets behind the suburbs to the west. Come at sunrise for the sun-over-ocean show; at sunset, watch the pink afterglow light up the eastern sky and the cliffs instead.

items.q: What's the best spot for sunrise at Bondi?
items.a: My pick is Mackenzies Point, the south headland at the start of the Bondi to Bronte walk, for the view back across the whole beach. The promenade above Bondi Icebergs is best for the classic ocean-pool-and-sky photo.

items.q: What time is sunrise and sunset at Bondi?
items.a: It shifts through the year — sunrise ranges from roughly 5:40am in midsummer to about 7am in winter. Check Geoscience Australia's sun times tool for the exact time on your date rather than guessing.

items.q: Might I see whales while watching the sunrise?
items.a: Possibly, roughly between May and November during the humpback migration. Mackenzies Point is one of the better clifftop vantage points — bring binoculars and scan the horizon.

items.q: Do I need to pay or book?
items.a: No. Every spot here is free public headland or promenade. The only thing worth checking ahead is Bondi Icebergs' pool session times if you plan to swim, as those change seasonally.

blocks.text: Whichever end you choose, put your phone down for the last few minutes. There's a particular hush at Bondi just as the sky turns — joggers slow, surfers sit up on their boards, and the whole beach seems to hold its breath. That's the bit you'll remember.

blocks.text: Bondi doesn't do the glossy, velvet-rope nightlife you might expect from a beach this famous — and that's exactly why I love a night out here. After dark it's more salt-in-your-hair pub sessions, ocean-view cocktails and long tables of people who came for one drink and stayed for five. Here's how I'd map a night, from a golden-hour beer to the last gelato before bed.
Where I start: sunset drinks with a view

The first hour of any Bondi night belongs to the water. My go-to is the bar upstairs at Icebergs on Notts Avenue — it looks straight down the length of the beach, and there's no better place to watch the light go pink over the pool. It's a special-occasion sort of price, so I nurse one negroni and soak it in. For something more low-key, Ravesi's on the corner of Campbell Parade and Hall Street has a classic beachside public bar and a terrace that catches the last of the sun.

Sunset seats at the ocean-view spots go fast on a clear evening. If you want the bar upstairs at Icebergs or a terrace table at Ravesi's, get there a good hour before the sun drops — or book ahead where the venue allows it.
The heart of the night: pubs & bars
This is where Bondi really is itself. A few of my regular haunts:

The Royal Bondi — a grand corner pub on Bondi Road, now run by Merivale. There's regular live music, and the front bar has pool tables and the footy on; upstairs turns into a proper dancefloor on weekends.
Ravesi's — beyond the beachside public bar downstairs, the upstairs bar runs DJ sets on weekends. Check their site for the current line-up before you head up.
Neighbourhood Bondi — exposed brick, good wine and cocktails, and the kind of buzzy-but-not-deafening room where you can actually hear your mates talk.
North Bondi — the northern end has easy, unpretentious spots for a beer close to the sand; it's my pick when I want the beach in view but the fuss dialled right down.

blocks.title: A quick reality check on 'nightclubs'
blocks.text: Bondi isn't a big-club district — the scene is pub- and bar-led, with weekend DJ sets rather than dedicated superclubs. If you want a heavy club night, most locals hop a rideshare to the city or the Inner West. In Bondi, the pubs are the party.
Live music

For live bands, The Royal is the most reliable bet right in Bondi, with regular gigs through the week. A short trip up the hill, the venues around Bondi Junction and Oxford Street add more stages if you're chasing a specific act. Whatever you're into, check the venue's own What's On page for the night you're coming — line-ups change constantly and I never trust a months-old listing.
Late-night eats & getting home

No Bondi night ends without a feed. Gelato Messina is my sweet-tooth default, and the beach end of Hall Street and Campbell Parade keeps a few kitchens going for a post-drinks slice or burger. Hours shift with the season, so don't bank on any one place being open past midnight midweek.

blocks.title: Plan your ride home before you go out
blocks.text: Bondi is not on the train line — the nearest station is Bondi Junction, roughly 3km uphill. Late at night you're relying on night buses or rideshare, and surge pricing on a warm Saturday is real. Check the Transport for NSW trip planner for current night services before you leave.

items.q: Does Bondi Beach have a nightclub scene?
items.a: Not in the big-superclub sense. Bondi's nightlife runs on pubs and bars with weekend DJ sets and live music — places like The Royal and Ravesi's. For a dedicated club night, most people head into the city or the Inner West.

items.q: Which nights are best for going out in Bondi?
items.a: Thursday to Sunday. Weekends bring the DJs and the biggest crowds, while Thursday and Sunday afternoons are great for a more relaxed live-music session.

items.q: Where can I get a drink with a view of the beach?
items.a: The bar upstairs at Icebergs has the standout ocean outlook, and Ravesi's has a beachside terrace on Campbell Parade. Both fill up at sunset, so arrive early on clear evenings.

items.q: How do I get home from Bondi late at night?
items.a: Bondi has no train station — the nearest is Bondi Junction, about 3km uphill. After the last buses, rideshare is the usual option. Check the Transport for NSW trip planner for current night-bus times.

items.q: Is there live music in Bondi?
items.a: Yes — The Royal on Bondi Road hosts live bands several nights a week, and there are more stages up around Bondi Junction. Always check the venue's What's On page for the specific night you're visiting.

blocks.text: That's a Bondi night as I'd do it: a drink with the ocean still glowing, a proper pub in the middle, and something sweet before the walk home. It's not flashy — it's just genuinely good fun, with sand still between your toes. See you out there.
